'''Barry M. Trost''' (born June 13, 1941, in [[Philadelphia]]) is an American chemist who is the Job and Gertrud Tamaki Professor Emeritus in the School of Humanities and Sciences at [[Stanford University]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|title=Barry Trost {{!}} Department of Chemistry|url=https://chemistry.stanford.edu/people/barry-trost|access-date=May 24, 2021|website=chemistry.stanford.edu}}</ref> The [[Tsuji–Trost reaction]] and the [[Trost ligand]] are named after him. He is prominent for advancing the concept of [[atom economy]].<ref>{{cite journal|last=Trost|first=Barry M.|year=1991|title=Atom Economy: A Search for Synthetic Efficiency|journal=[[Science (journal)|Science]]|volume=254|issue=5037|pages=1471–1477|bibcode=1991Sci...254.1471T|doi=10.1126/science.1962206|pmid=1962206}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last=Trost|first=Barry M.|year=1995|title=Atom Economy - A Challenge for Organic Synthesis: Homogeneous Catalysis Leads the Way|journal=[[Angewandte Chemie International Edition]]|volume=34|issue=3|pages=259–281|doi=10.1002/anie.199502591}}</ref> <!-- His research interests revolve around the theme of selectivity, developing new reactions and reagents that are chemo-, regio-, diastereo-, and enantioselective and new synthetic strategies for the total synthesis of bioactive and novel molecules. -->

== Early life and education ==
Trost was born in [[Philadelphia|Philadelphia, Pennsylvania]] on June 13, 1941. He studied at the [[University of Pennsylvania]] and obtained his B.A. in 1962.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last1=Trost|first1=Barry M.|last2=Toste|first2=F. Dean|last3=Pinkerton|first3=Anthony B.|date=June 19, 2001|title=Non-Metathesis Ruthenium-Catalyzed C−C Bond Formation|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/full/10.1021/cr000666b|journal=Chemical Reviews|volume=101|issue=7|pages=2067–2096|doi=10.1021/cr000666b|pmid=11710241|issn=0009-2665|url-access=subscription}}</ref> He then attended the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] for graduate school, where he worked with [[Herbert O. House]] on [[Enolate|enolate anions]], the [[Mannich reaction]], and the [[Robinson annulation]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=House|first1=Herbert O.|last2=Trost|first2=Barry M.|date=June 1, 1964|title=The Mannich Reaction with 2-Methylcyclopentanone and 2-Methylcyclo hexanone1a|url=https://doi.org/10.1021/jo01029a016|journal=The Journal of Organic Chemistry|volume=29|issue=6|pages=1339–1341|doi=10.1021/jo01029a016|issn=0022-3263|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=House|first1=Herbert O.|last2=Trost|first2=Barry M.|date=May 1, 1965|title=The Chemistry of Carbanions. IX. The Potassium and Lithium Enolates Derived from Cyclic Ketones1|url=https://doi.org/10.1021/jo01016a001|journal=The Journal of Organic Chemistry|volume=30|issue=5|pages=1341–1348|doi=10.1021/jo01016a001|issn=0022-3263|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=House|first1=Herbert O.|last2=Trost|first2=Barry M.|last3=Magin|first3=Ralph W.|last4=Carlson|first4=Robert G.|last5=Franck|first5=Richard W.|last6=Rasmusson|first6=Gary H.|date=August 1, 1965|title=By-products of the Robinson Annelation Reaction with Cyclohexanone, Cyclopentanone, and Cyclopentane-1,2-dione1|url=https://doi.org/10.1021/jo01019a004|journal=The Journal of Organic Chemistry|volume=30|issue=8|pages=2513–2519|doi=10.1021/jo01019a004|issn=0022-3263|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Trost graduated with his Ph.D. in 1965.

== Independent career ==
Trost moved to the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]] to begin his independent career, and was promoted to professor of chemistry in 1969, and the Vilas Research Professor in 1982.<ref name=":0" /> In 1987, he moved to [[Stanford University]] as professor of chemistry, and was appointed the Job and Gertrud Tamaki Professor of Humanities and Sciences in 1990. He previously served as chair of the department of chemistry.<ref name=":0" /> 

<!-- In 1994, he was presented with a Docteur Honoris Causa of the Université Claude-Bernard (Lyon I), France and, in 1997, with a Doctor Scientiarium Honoris Causa of the Technion, Haifa, Israel. In recognition of his many contributions, he has received a number of awards, including the ACS Award in Pure Chemistry (1977), the ACS Award for Creative Work in Synthetic Organic Chemistry (1981), the Baekeland Award (1981), Arthur C. Cope Scholar Award (1989), Guenther Award in the Chemistry of Essential Oils and Related Products (1990), the Dr. Paul Janssen Prize (1990), the ASSU Graduate Teaching Award (1991), Bing Teaching Award (1993), the ACS Roger Adams Award (1995), the Herbert C. Brown Award for Creative Research in Synthetic Methods, American Chemical Society (1999), the Belgian Organic Synthesis Symposium Elsevier Award (2000), the Nichols Medal (2000), and the Yamada Prize (2001). He was elected a Fellow of the American Academy of Sciences (1982) and a member of the National Academy of Sciences (1980). He coordinates the ACS course “Frontiers in Organic Chemistry.” He edited a major compendium entitled Comprehensive Organic Synthesis consisting of nine volumes and serves as editor for ChemTracts/Organic Chemistry. -->
{{As of|2026|6|df=US}}, Trost has an [[h-index]] of 179 according to [[Google Scholar]]<ref>{{Google Scholar id}}</ref> and of 154 (1042 documents) according to [[Scopus]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.scopus.com/authid/detail.uri?authorId=57217139833|title=Scopus preview – Trost, Barry M. – Author details – Scopus|website=www.scopus.com|accessdate=October 17, 2021}}</ref>

==Research==
Trost's research focused on chemical synthesis.<ref name="Stanford University 2017">{{cite web | title=Trost Group Home | website=Stanford University | date=30 March 2017 | url=https://web.stanford.edu/group/bmtrost/ | access-date=17 October 2021}}</ref> In order to build complex target molecules from simple molecules, Trost developed new reactions and reagents, and utilized [[cascade reaction]]s and tandem reactions.<ref name="Stanford University 2017" /> Target molecules have potential applications as novel catalysts, as well as antibiotic and anti-tumor therapeutics.<ref name=":1" />
